content.p: The Sureños are not a gang in the way a single street crew is. They are a loose movement of hundreds of Hispanic gangs, born in California prisons and street neighbourhoods, that share a name, a number and a loyalty to one prison gang: the Mexican Mafia, known as La Eme. A 2008 law-enforcement gang report describes the structure as very loose, with no formal rank system but with well-known veterans and "shot callers" who carry influence. The report counts 18th Street, Florencia 13 and Mara Salvatrucha among its "super" gangs.

The federal cases described here were brought against particular cliques and networks, not against the Sureños as a whole. Federal prosecutors have brought racketeering cases against a Los Angeles street gang and its lawyer, a large Los Angeles County jail enterprise, and, in October 2025, nine alleged members of the Oakland Sureños. Everyone named below as charged is presumed innocent unless a court has convicted them, and the text says where a court has.

Police Magazine's 2000 account traces the movement to the 1950s. It says that in 1956 and 1957 East Los Angeles gang members including Guero "Buff" Flores served time at the Duel Vocational Institute and together formed the "gang of gangs", La Eme, California's first prison gang. The article says it formed partly for protection and recruited from Mexican street gangs. By 1967, it says, La Eme was trying to unite all the Mexicans in the state.

The split came a year later. In the magazine's telling, a murder at San Quentin in 1968 over a stolen pair of shoes, in which an original La Eme member stabbed a Northern California roommate, hardened an existing rivalry between Mexicans from the north and the south of the state. The northerners formed a second prison gang, Nuestra Familia, to protect themselves from La Eme. IBTimes UK dates the emergence of the Sureños to 1968 as well, and says the name was not used until 1970, after mass brawls in and out of prisons. The two accounts are not identical, and the shoes story is one gang expert's version rather than a court finding.

Numbers and colours followed. The magazine says Northern gangs took the number 14, for the fourteenth letter, N, for Norteño. Southern gangs took 13, the letter M, which in Spanish is "eme". They tattooed 13 and the words Sureño or Sur on their bodies. Northerners claimed red, the article says, because most southern inmates had chosen the blue railroad handkerchief. The 2000 article says the dividing line was usually placed somewhere between Bakersfield and Delano; the 2008 report says it is generally recognised as near Delano, though others put it at Bakersfield or elsewhere in Kern County.

The 2008 report adds that every Hispanic gang in California is expected to claim one side or the other. It names the Fresno Bulldogs as the exception, a gang strong enough to stay independent of both. It also names an exception inside the south. The Maravilla gangs of East Los Angeles are not counted as Sureños. The report says some Maravilla members grew disillusioned with the early Mexican Mafia and refused to pay it taxes, and that the Mafia answered with a "green light", a kill-on-sight order. It says Maravilla inmates had to be kept apart from Mexican Mafia and Sureño sympathisers in the Los Angeles County jail, and that the report is not consistent on the order's fate: one passage says it was recalled only recently, another that it has not been lifted.

What binds the clique-level gangs together is tribute. The 2010 Police Magazine column, written by a gang-crime expert who has testified in trials, says Florencia 13, 18th Street and Mara Salvatrucha all pay taxes to the Mexican Mafia and obey its codes. It also says that in 1993 the Mafia issued three edicts to Southern California's Hispanic street gangs: take over drug areas formerly held by Black gangs, tax illegal-alien drug dealers working in Sureño territory, and stop drive-by shootings. The edicts were publicised as a "Hispanic peace initiative". The author's view is that the aim was to cut the collateral casualties that brought police attention, not to stop killing; he says gangs were encouraged to keep killing face to face.

The same column describes what happened to a gang that broke the drive-by rule, an account that rests on its author alone. In October 1995, the author says, three Florencia 13 members drove up to a house in Huntington Park and one of them fired an AK-47 from the car, killing an 11-year-old girl on her porch and wounding two boys aged 15 and 14. Ten days later, the author says, a Mexican Mafia member visited two of the shooters and demanded to know who had fired. They named the third man. The Mafia member, the article says, ordered them to kill him or put the entire gang on the green-light list. They killed him at his mother's door on a Saturday morning, were arrested the same day and, the author says, were convicted and given long prison terms.

The 2008 National Drug Intelligence Center report to Congress shows the money side. Citing reports from law enforcement officials, it says Tijuana Cartel members work with high-ranking Mexican Mafia associates in controlling the drug trafficking of Hispanic street gang members it calls Sureños 13 in the Pacific and Southwest regions. It also says Gulf Cartel traffickers were supplying drugs to Sureños 13 street gang members in a number of cities and suburbs across the Midwest and Southwest.

Police Magazine's 2000 article says that by the late 1980s and early 1990s most southwestern states had noted gangs calling themselves Sureño or Sureño-13, and that states to the north of California had begun to see Sureño and Norteño gangs in the late 1980s. Many of those groups, it says, had no formal connection to traditional Southern California gangs, and some had roots tracing back to California only through migrating members. IBTimes UK reported in 2014, without naming a source, about 30,000 members, and said the gang was "recruiting new blood at its fastest rate ever". That report accompanied a Homeland Security crackdown in which Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials said more than 600 people were arrested across almost 200 cities, targeting 175 gangs including the Sureños.
The cases below are federal racketeering prosecutions, each aimed at one clique or one Mexican Mafia network.

Columbia Lil' Cycos. The Los Angeles FBI office describes the Columbia Lil' Cycos as a clique of the 18th Street gang that, according to court documents and trial evidence, used violence and intimidation to control narcotics sales near MacArthur Park in the Westlake District. Dealers and street vendors paid "rent" for permission to sell and protection from rivals, and the clique collected tens of thousands of dollars a week. On 15 September 2007 a vendor who had refused a $50 payment was shot four times and survived; a 23-day-old baby sleeping in a stroller beside him was struck and killed. Forty-three members and associates were charged in a 2009 federal indictment. The FBI says 37 have been convicted and six are fugitives.

One of those convicted was a lawyer. Isaac Guillen, a former gang member who attended law school at UCLA, was sentenced to 84 months in federal prison for racketeering and money laundering. The FBI says he admitted that he used attorney-client privilege to carry the clique's messages to and from a convicted Mexican Mafia member serving multiple life sentences at the federal "supermax" prison in Florence, Colorado, and that he laundered more than $1.3 million in drug and extortion money. Law&Crime reports that a jury convicted him in 2012.

Puente-13. In September 2017 the Ninth Circuit affirmed the racketeering and drug-conspiracy convictions and sentences of four defendants tied to Puente-13. The opinion describes a gang with about 600 documented members by 2010 that carved out a territorial monopoly on drug sales and demanded "taxes" from dealers; those who bought elsewhere or refused to pay were attacked or excluded. It says the gang was subordinate to the Mexican Mafia, paid it a share of its revenue and served as its street-level enforcer. A footnote records trial testimony that a "sureño" is a soldier for the Mexican Mafia. The investigation, by the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, began in the early 2000s.

Operation Dirty Thirds. On 23 May 2018, more than 500 law-enforcement personnel took part in an operation that put 32 defendants in custody, among 83 charged in two federal racketeering indictments. Thirty-five were already in custody and 16 were fugitives. One indictment alleged that Mexican Mafia members controlled drug smuggling, sales and extortion inside the Los Angeles County jail system, including a "kitty" built from a percentage of Latino inmates' commissary spending. The name came from a rule, described by prosecutors, that others in a facility could not sell drugs until a Mexican Mafia member had sold his "thirds". The indictment named Jose Landa-Rodriguez as a leader. A second indictment concerned an alleged enterprise run by an imprisoned Mexican Mafia member over Pomona-area gangs. The prosecutors' statement stressed that an indictment contains allegations only.

A defendant in the jail case, the attorney Gabriel Zendejas-Chavez, was accused of carrying orders and the names of suspected informants between prisons. He went to trial in August 2022. The prosecution's star witness, Luis "Hefty" Garcia, whom Law&Crime describes as a former top-ranking Sureño in the jails, testified that he had been running the jails with Landa-Rodriguez and hoped to shed a possible life sentence for attempted murder by cooperating. Law&Crime noted that the Mexican Mafia then had about 140 full members.

Oakland. The most recent case is in Northern California. An indictment filed on 9 October 2025 and unsealed on 29 October charges nine men with racketeering conspiracy, tied to the Oakland Sureños, which prosecutors say recognised the primacy of the Mexican Mafia. It lists two 2019 murders of men seen as rivals, three attempted murders, and drug and firearms trafficking. Six were arrested that morning, two were already in custody and one, Gonzalo Pablo, was at large. The maximum for the conspiracy count is 20 years; the allegations against six men carry a maximum of life. They had been due to be arraigned the next day. The prosecutors' statement said the men are presumed innocent until proven guilty.
